rows.gloss: a kind of war-drum or kettledrum
rows.etymology: 92. OIA lex. drakaṭa- and dragaḍa- ‘a kettle-drum for awakening sleepers’ has modern reflexes (all with preservation of medial single stop) in Kṭg. drāg ‘a particular type of drum’, MKH drag ‘music’, Kiũṭh. durāgī ‘a kind of loud drum’ — B. dagaḍ ‘a kind of war-drum or kettledrum’, A. dɒgɒr ‘small drum’ — Mult. dragṛī ‘a chapātī baked on one side only. With the unbaked side covered with ghī and placed next the hair it is bound on the head as a cure for head-ache’, and Psht. dūkṛah ‘a kind of kettle drum’. The words reflect an old synonym formation, cf. OIA lex. dardara- ‘a kind of drum’ and dardura- ‘the sound of a drum’, and karaṭa- (comment on VarBr̥S.) ‘a kind of drum’ and OIA ghaṭā- or perhaps ghaṭa- ‘a kind of drum’ with typical tenuis versus aspirated media opposition. The second component karaṭa- may have been either borrowed into Tocharian *kera ‘some sort of musical instrument (?)’ respectively kerū* ‘drum’ but Adams (1999) suggests that the words are connected “with an Indo-European group meaning ‘cauldron, kettle”’ like OIA carú- ‘kettle, pot, pan’, Old Irish coire ‘kettle’, etc., thus ultimately going back to PIE *kȗer-² ‘a kind of dish or pot’ and ‘in words meaning s.th. like a dish or bowl’ (IEW: 642) (which fits with the Mult. meaning) even though there are phonological problems. Adams also mentions Toch.A karel ‘drum’ which is related but must have a somehow different PIE origin. All data suggest a complex origin for the IA, Ir. and Toch. forms.

rows.etymology: 6. Bur. ġaḍaġaḍáp ‘sound of horse’s hooves’, Sh. gaṛáp ‘ditto’, Ind. gʌṛʌ́p-gʌṛʌpʰ ‘sound of clatter (of horses)’ — Bng. gɔṛɔp-gɔṛɔp ‘sound of clatter of horses’ — Sant. kaʈaʔp kaʈaʔp ‘clattering (sound of hoofed animals walking; of wooden clogs)’. Notes:  (a) The gaṛáp lemma has, with the exception of Bng., the accent on the su- perordinate syllable. It is thus sesquisyllabic. I found association of the sound gaṛáp with the gait of a horse or hoofed animal only in Burushaski, Dardic, Baṅgāṇī and Munda. And even though one can always overlook something, I did not find convincing parallels in Mon-Khmer, Dravidian, Tibeto-Burman or Iranian. The somewhat similar ideophone M. gaḍagaḍaṇēṃ ‘to clatter’ seems not to be associated with horse gait. Whereas gaṛáp has a sesquisyllabic struc- ture CVCV́ C, Marāṭhī gaḍagaḍa- does not have this; there is instead CVCV. Nevertheless, that sesquisyllabic word structures, which are a characteristic of Austro-Asiatic, must have had their impact on Indo-Aryan also in the field of ideophones, is demonstrated by the following example: Hindi and Panjābī dapaṭ mean also ‘gallop’ besides ‘rush; attack (commonly used in compounds with dauṛ- ‘run’)’ but, of course, their second syllable is not superordinate. They have a morphological near-parallel in Prasun dəpˈak, ḍəpˈak ‘hustling with force and vehemence’, here with sesquisyllabic structure because of the accent. Hindi dapaṭ is derived by Platts < Pk. dabaḍī- < OIA DRAV ‘run, hasten’ (cf. also Pa. davo- ‘quick motion’, Pk. davadavā- ‘veg vālī gati – swift motion’ [Sheth: A com- prehensive Prakrit-Hindi dictionary] and Old G. davadavāe ‘with speed’ [6623 dravá- ‘quick motion’], and S. ḍrokaṇu ‘to gallop’ [6624 drávati ‘runs’]). The Hindi word is not found in the CDIAL because Turner must have thought that Platts’ derivation < OIA drava- + -ṭa- could not be correct. But we have seen in many cases that both in Munda and in different Outer Languages voice fluctua- tions are quite common (cf. e.g. Kt. tapip ‘doctor’ ← Ar. t̤abīb). Therefore the Hindi and Panjābī word must be a borrowing from an Outer Language – cf. here again Prasun dəpˈak, ḍəpˈak – which had used an Indo-Aryan lexeme to which an ‘ideophoneme’ -ṭ was suffixed in order to form an ideophone based on the very common Munda/Mon-Khmer morphological pattern of sesquisyllabicity. The morphological relationship between Bur. ġaḍaġaḍáp and M. gaḍagaḍaṇēṃ par- allels the morphological relationship between Prasun dəpˈak, ḍəpˈak and Prasun ḍəbəḍəbə ‘rumbling’ with regard to ± sesquisyllabicity. The latter word appears in the text published by Buddruss und Degener (2016) together with a verb of motion: ḍəbəḍəbə tī amˈaso ‘(he) comes rumbling’. Tellingly, Prasun ḍəbəḍəbə has also a sesquisyllabic-like allomorph ḍubeḍobˈi ‘rumbling’ which also qualifies in the text a verb of motion. We thus observe that an IA verb of motion (DRU) has been ‘ideophonized’ by using a Munda/Mon-Khmer pattern of sesquisyllab- icity created with the help of ‘ideophoneme’ suffixes so that it then can qualify other verbs of motion. The remaining question is, whether a similar historical development can be discovered in case of Santali kaʈaʔp kaʈaʔp ‘clattering’. I provisionally suggest derivation < Proto-Kherwarian (North.Munda) *kaʈa ‘leg’ (see SEAlang) which is, so to say, a noun of motion, and which is typically used e.g. in Sant. mɛrɔm kaʈa ‘goat’s trotters’, sukri kaʈa ‘pig’s trotters’, both of which are hoofed animals. So there can hardly be any doubt that the Bur., Sh., Bng. and Ind. words are direct borrowings from Munda. Last of all, this is fur- ther supported by Bur. gaṭál ‘by foot’ as in gaṭál bulá ‘polo by foot (played by children)’ and kaṭál ‘on foot’ (Willson), which also most probably is a borrow- ing of Munda kaʈa ‘leg’, and where also the second word bulá shows the typical tendency in Burushaski for voicing of unvoiced stops in borrowings. (b) Note also quite similar Pers. ǰugúp-ǰugúp ‘sound of hooves’ (Degener) which is not etymologically connected with the above lemma.

rows.etymology: 1. The Bangāṇī God of Thunder is called guṛku (also meaning ‘thunder’) which is < OIA *guḍ- ‘rumble’ (4180) with a modern parallel in S. to which have to be added Thar. gurgurāi ‘thunder’, Kann. gŭrgŭr ‘thunder’, K. gur-gur ‘a rumble, thunder’ and gagrāy, gɨgrāray ‘thunder’ (Sachdeva et al. [2010: 56]), Klm. āga-guṛant HL-LH ‘it is thundering’ (lit. ‘the sky is thundering’), Garh. gagṛāṭ and giṛaktāḷ ‘thunder’, Ko.S. guḍguḍu ‘thunderbolt’, Ko.kaṇ. guḍguḍ ‘thunder’, and M. gaḍagaḍaṇeṃ ‘to thunder’ — Sant. guɖ guɖ ‘droning, rolling, rumbling (sound of thunder, railway, drums, a running flock of animals, of a water cataract)’, Gtaˈ guɽuŋ-geɽeeke ‘thunder’ — Ora. guṛguṛnā ‘thunder’. Notes: (a) Ju. goɭgoɭi ‘thunder’ reflects OIA (Bālar.) gulugulita- ‘the roaring (of an ele- phant)’, OIA gulagulā- ‘thunder’, gulagulāyate ‘thunders’ (Pa., Pk., but not men- tioned in CDIAL) with Dravidian reflexes found sub DEDR 1837 Ma. guḷūguḷū ‘sound of fruits falling into water’. It appears obvious that the OIA words are borrowings from Munda. Thus, Munda Ju., Dravidian Ma. (and its Dravidian parallels) were borrowed from Munda via an Indo-Aryan language. (b) Note also PN *gur- ‘to rumble, roar, growl, gurgle’ (CINCL 393), PIE *gʰur- ‘to rumble’, according to Bomhard reflected in OIA ghuraghurāyate ‘to utter gur- gling sounds’ (recte ghurghurā- ‘continual growling; Geknurre’ which Mayrhofer characterizes as onomatopoeia which no-one can doubt), cf. also Bomhard’s quotes (ibid.) of Pk. ghurukhaï ‘to thunder’ and S. guguravanā ‘to thunder’. (c) Note also Kartvelian *gurgw- in Georgian grgv-in-v-a ‘to thunder’, Mingre- lian gurg- in gurg-in-i ‘to thunder’, Laz girg-, gurg- in girg-in-i ‘to thunder’ and Svan gurgw- in li-gurgw-n-i ‘to thunder’.
